title: Supreme Court of Judicature (Amendment No 2) Bill
what_it_is: Supreme Court of Judicature (Amendment No 2) Bill

sections.label: Electronic court hearings
sections.summary: Clause 2 provides that Courts can conduct hearings via electronic means such as live video or television link.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 2 of the Bill, therefore, provides that the Courts can conduct hearings via electronic means, such as live video link or live television link.

sections.label: Court of Appeal written submissions
sections.summary: The provision proposes the Court of Appeal can determine any application and, with parties' consent, Singapore International Commercial Court appeals based on written submissions.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Under this provision, it is now proposed that the Court of Appeal can determine (a) any application, and (b) in circumstances where parties consent, appeals from the Singapore International Commercial Court, based on written submissions.

sections.label: Summary dismissal by Court of Appeal
sections.summary: Clause 7 empowers the Court of Appeal on its own motion to summarily dismiss certain matters in two situations.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Second, clause 7 empowers the Court of Appeal on its own motion to summarily dismiss certain matters in two situations.

sections.label: Leave for further evidence
sections.summary: Clause 9 proposes leave of Court be required before applying to admit further evidence on appeal, except matters occurring after the decision date.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: This is, of course, with the exception of matters or evidence which occurred after the date of decision as parties would not obviously have known about it.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Therefore, in this vein, clause 9 of the Bill proposes that leave of Court would be required before an application can be made to admit further evidence on appeal, except for matters which occurred subsequent to the date of decision.

sections.label: Appeal monetary threshold increase
sections.summary: Clause 3 increases the monetary threshold to $60,000 for District and Magistrates' Courts decisions appealable with leave to the High Court.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: On the first point, clause 3 increases the monetary threshold to $60,000 for decisions of the District and Magistrates’ Courts which are appealable with leave to the High Court.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: At present, as some Members may know, decisions of the District and Magistrates’ Courts are appealable to the High Court with leave if the amount in dispute does not exceed $50,000.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: However, the jurisdiction of the Magistrates’ Court is set at $60,000, which means that there are cases with claim values between $50,000 and $60,000 which would be appealable to the High Court without leave.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The proposed amendment just seeks to ensure consistency and provides that there will be no automatic right of appeal for cases that fall within the $50,000 to $60,000 range.

sections.label: Civil restraint orders
sections.summary: Clause 10 introduces a new power allowing Courts to make three types of civil restraint orders to address varying degrees of vexatious conduct.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: To address these limitations, clause 10 of the Bill introduces a new power to allow the Courts to make three different types of civil restraint orders to address varying degrees of vexatious conduct.

sections.label: Restraint on commencing actions
sections.summary: A party is restrained from starting actions or applications on matters tied to the proceedings, without leave of Court, for up to two years.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The party will be restrained from commencing any action or making any application concerning any matter involving, relating to, touching upon or leading to the proceedings in which the order is made, without leave of Court for a period not exceeding two years.

sections.label: Orders under proposed amendments
sections.summary: The High Court or Court of Appeal may make orders on its own motion, on a party's application, or on the Attorney-General's application.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Under the proposed amendments, the High Court or Court of Appeal may make these orders: (a) on its own motion, which it presently cannot do; (b) on an application by a party, again, which it presently cannot do; or (c) on an application by the Attorney-General, which is the current position envisaged under section 74.

sections.label: Late filing fees
sections.summary: Clause 16 lets Courts impose late filing fees for non-compliance with Rules of Court, Court orders or directions and practice directions.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: In addition to the powers to manage vexatious proceedings, clause 16 of the Bill also ensures the efficient disposal of cases by allowing the Courts to impose late filing fees for non-compliance with the Rules of Court, Court orders or directions and practice directions.

sections.label: Hearings via live video
sections.summary: Clauses 2 and 19 enable the Court of Appeal and High Court to conduct hearings via live video technology.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Launched in 2013, the eLitigation system gave a better overview of the case compared to the previous Electronic Filing System, which was more document-centric.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the same vein, clauses 2 and 19 of this Bill enables the Court of Appeal and the High Court to conduct hearings via live video technology.

sections.label: Tools against vexatious litigation
sections.summary: Clauses 10 and 11 introduce a greater range of tools to vexatious litigation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clauses 10 and 11 introduce a greater range of tools to vexatious litigation.

sections.label: New evidence on appeal
sections.summary: Clause 9 restricts new evidence that may be tendered on appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clause 9 restricts new evidence that may be tendered on appeal.

sections.label: Interlocutory appeals and categorisation rationale
sections.summary: The middle category of interlocutory orders may be appealed to the Court of Appeal only with leave, and the speaker asks whether the categorisation rationale has changed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The middle category which consists of orders made at interlocutory applications which lie in the middle of these two extreme situations may be appealed to the Court of Appeal only with leave of Court." In light of this, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State whether the rationale behind the categorisations has changed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The amendments in this Bill are important as they provide the flexibility and tools for the administration of justice to adapt with the times, not to dilute the administration of justice but to ensure the processes remain efficient and effective.

sections.label: Amendments seen as limiting right to be heard
sections.summary: The Bill proposes amendments perceived by some as limiting a litigant's right to be heard, including leave requirements and summary dismissal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Bill also proposes a number of other amendments, which have been perceived by some members of the public as imposing limits on a litigant's right to be heard.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: These amendments include requiring leave of Court before an application can be made to admit further evidence on appeal, allowing the Court of Appeal to determine a broader range of matters based on written submission, and allowing the Court of Appeal to summarily dismiss appeals or applications on its own motions.

sections.label: Minister decides appealable civil matters
sections.summary: The amendment lets the Minister, in consultation with the Chief Justice, decide changes to the Schedule without Parliament passing them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The amendment moves the determination of appealable civil matters further from Parliamentary scrutiny.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Changes to the Schedule can be decided by the Minister in consultation with the Chief Justice, as the Senior Minister of State has mentioned in his speech, without needing to be passed through Parliament.

sections.label: Extended civil restraint order provision
sections.summary: New section 73C provides for an extended civil restraint order restraining an individual from commencing actions or applications concerning the legal proceedings at hand.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The new section 73C provides for an extended civil restraint order which restraints an individual from commencing an action or making an application which concerns any matter "involving, relating to, touching upon or leading to" the legal proceedings at hand.

sections.label: Clarification sought on extension factors
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Senior Minister of State to elaborate on factors for determining whether an extension is appropriate, while supporting the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Senior Minister of State also elaborate on the circumstances or factors to be considered in determining whether an extension is appropriate?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Nonetheless, flexibility should be exercised in a principled manner that respects the individual's right to be heard.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I hope the Senior Minister of State will be able to clarify the above matters and provide litigants with greater clarity on when the provisions may or may not apply.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the above concerns and clarifications requested, I do stand in support of the Bill.

sections.label: Refusal of leave is final
sections.summary: An order of a Judge of Appeal sitting alone refusing leave to adduce fresh evidence is final.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: An order of a Judge of Appeal sitting alone refusing leave to adduce fresh evidence is final.

sections.label: Minister amends SCJA Schedules
sections.summary: Proposed section 83(1) of the SCJA lets the Minister amend the Third to Sixth Schedules by Gazette after consulting the Chief Justice, unlike section 34(3).

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The proposed section 83(1) of the SCJA vests with the Minister the powers to amend the Third, Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Schedule via the Gazette after consulting the Chief Justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This compares differently from section 34(3) where it is provided that the President may, after consulting the Chief Justice, amend the Court jurisdictional money limits, again, via the Gazette.

sections.label: High Court assigns lawyers
sections.summary: Under section 74(2) of the SCJA, the High Court has powers to assign a lawyer to a party who cannot afford one.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The significant difference is that under section 74(2) of SCJA, the High Court has powers to assign a lawyer to the party who cannot afford to pay for a lawyer.

sections.label: Shifting non-appealable matters
sections.summary: It shifts non-appealable matters in section 34(1) to the Fourth Schedule and appealable-with-leave matters in section 34(2) to the Fifth Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: As Mr Louis Ng and Mr Murali Pillai and I think also Mr Christopher de Souza have noted, it shifts matters which are non-appealable in section 34(1) to the Fourth Schedule, and those which are appealable with leave from section 34(2) to the Fifth Schedule.

sections.label: Schedules revisited by Minister
sections.summary: The Schedules will be revisited from time to time and added to or removed from by the Minister in consultation with the Chief Justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Schedules will be revisited from time to time, and added to or removed from, by the Minister, in consultation with the Chief Justice.

sections.label: President amends monetary limits
sections.summary: It is consistent with sections 30 and 53(2) of the State Courts Act, where the President amends monetary limits after consulting the Chief Justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The reason, I referred to it in my original speech, is because it is consistent with sections 30 and 53(2) respectively of the State Courts Act, where it is the President who has the power to amend the monetary limits for the District Court and the Magistrates' Court, after consulting the Chief Justice.

sections.label: Further evidence needs leave
sections.summary: Parties are encouraged to put all available evidence before the Courts, and further evidence otherwise available earlier will only be allowed if leave is granted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To that extent, the parties are encouraged, and I think quite rightly so, given the limited resources we have for hearing time, to ensure that all the available evidence would be before the Courts, before the hearing itself.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And so, to that extent, when one is seeking to include further evidence in the appeal where that evidence was otherwise available to the party before the lower Court hearing, one has to be very circumspect about it and, in those situations, further evidence will only be allowed if leave is granted.

sections.label: SICC appeals without oral arguments
sections.summary: Section 34A(2) allows appeals from SICC judgments to be decided without oral arguments only if every party agrees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To ensure that this option is only exercised in cases where the parties consent, section 34A(2) provides that appeals from any judgments or order of the SICC can be decided without hearing oral arguments only if every party to the appeal agrees.

sections.label: Gradated approach and party applications
sections.summary: The amendments introduce a gradated approach to section 74 of the SCJA and allow parties other than the Attorney-General to apply.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: What is being sought to be introduced in these amendments are broadly two things: one, a gradated approach so that it is not a "one-size-fits-all" approach in section 74 of the SCJA as it is presently so; and second, it is to allow for parties, aside from the Attorney-General, to also make their application.

sections.label: Section 74 orders in 2017 and 2018
sections.summary: In 2017 only four orders were made under section 74 of the SCJA, and none have been made in 2018 to date.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In 2017, only four orders were made under section 74 of SCJA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To date, no such orders have been made in 2018.

sections.label: Extending civil restraint orders
sections.summary: The Court may extend an extended or general civil restraint order on its own motion or on application by the Attorney-General or a party.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Court may exercise its power to extend the period for which an extended or general civil restraint order remains in effect on its own motion, or on the application of the Attorney-General or a party to the proceedings.

sections.label: Appealing a civil restraint order
sections.summary: Under section 73A(9), a party subject to a civil restraint order may appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Under section 73A(9), a party against whom a civil restraint order is made may bring an appeal to the Court of Appeal with the leave of the High Court or the Court of Appeal.

sections.label: New orders complement section 74
sections.summary: The new civil restraint orders complement, not replace, section 74 powers, which provide measures and flexibility for dealing with vexatious litigants.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The new civil restraint orders seek to complement, but not replace, the current powers conferred on the Courts by section 74.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Section 74 does provide for a suite of measures to deal with vexatious litigants and allows the Court to have the flexibility of calibrating its response to the unique challenges posed by a particular case.

sections.label: No extension to criminal proceedings
sections.summary: The operation of civil restraint orders is not currently seen as needing extension to criminal proceedings, given section 74.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: At present, we do not see a need to extend the operation of such civil restraint orders to criminal proceedings, given that, as I said earlier, the presence of section 74 which can be used.

sections.label: Public Prosecutor discontinuing private prosecution
sections.summary: Under section 13 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the Public Prosecutor has the power to discontinue a private prosecution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In fact, under section 13 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC), the Public Prosecutor has the power to discontinue the private prosecution.

sections.label: Duration of section 74 orders
sections.summary: A section 74 order is in force indefinitely, while a general civil restraint order is in force for a maximum of two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: A section 74 order is in force indefinitely while a general civil restraint order, which is the most severe of the three types of orders that we now have, is in force for a maximum of two years.

sections.label: Policy underpinning both provisions
sections.summary: The policy underpinning both provisions is broadly similar: preventing abuse of Court processes and balancing litigants' access with protecting Courts and counterparties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Broadly speaking, the policy underpinning both provisions would be similar: to prevent abuse of Court processes and allow the Courts to strike a balance between giving effect to the rights of a litigant to have access to the Courts while protecting, on the other hand, the Courts and the counterparty from being inundated with the unmeritorious litigation to the detriment of other parties and also to the detriment of the efficient allocation and usage of Court resources.
